title: Designing, executing and interpreting test cases
learningObjectives: Derive test cases from requirements, function contracts, decision branches and boundary conditions.
Distinguish normal, boundary, invalid-input, failure-path and regression tests.
Create expected results independently of the implementation and compare actual results with them.
Use small deterministic tests to isolate defects and table-driven tests to cover multiple input/output pairs.
Interpret a failing test as evidence about a specific behaviour without changing the expected result merely to make the test pass.
Recognize the limits of testing: passing tests increase confidence but do not prove correctness for every possible input.

understand.concept: A test case supplies controlled input, performs an operation and checks the observed result against an expected result. A good test suite is derived from the specification and deliberately covers ordinary behaviour, boundaries and failure paths.
understand.whyItMatters: Without planned tests, developers tend to check only the example they already expect to work. Systematic tests expose off-by-one errors, incorrect conditions, missing error handling and regressions introduced by later changes.
understand.analogy: A quality inspector checks a product against a checklist, including normal operation and stress points. The checklist is written from requirements rather than adjusted after seeing a defect.
understand.analogyLimit: Tests can only check the cases and observations they contain. A test suite may miss a defect, and a passing run does not prove that all possible executions are correct.

explain.narrative:
Start with the contract and identify equivalence classes: groups of inputs expected to behave similarly. Select representative values from each group, then add boundary values immediately below, at and above important limits. Include empty and single-element cases where applicable, invalid input and simulated operational failures.

For each test, record a stable ID, purpose, input, expected result and observed result. Derive the expected result independently—by hand calculation, a trusted specification or a separate simple method. Do not copy the program's output into the expected column without checking it.

Run tests after each meaningful change. A failing test should be reproducible and small enough to diagnose. After fixing the defect, retain the test as a regression test. Table-driven tests make repeated input/output checks concise. Use compiler warnings, static analysis and sanitizers as complementary tools; none replaces tests or design reasoning.

examples.title: A deterministic table-driven test for a maximum function
examples.explanation: The test program checks positive values, all-negative values, an empty input and a missing output pointer. Each assertion is expressed as a nonzero process exit on failure, so a successful run returns zero. The expected maxima are determined directly from the small arrays.

examples.title: A test matrix for a bounded conversion requirement
examples.code:
/* Function contract: accept an integer from 1 through 100.

   Case ID     Input       Expected
   T-01        1           accept
   T-02        100         accept
   T-03        0           reject
   T-04        101         reject
   T-05        -1          reject
   T-06        nonnumeric  reject

   The matrix is written from the contract, not from observed output. */
examples.explanation: The table covers both inclusive boundaries and values just outside them, plus a malformed representation. The same matrix can become a table-driven C test after the conversion function is implemented.

practise.guidedTask: For a function that returns the position of a target in an array, design tests for an empty array, one item, first item, last item, absent item and repeated target. State whether the first or any matching position is required.
practise.independentTask: Create a test plan for a function that accepts a percentage from 0 through 100. Include boundaries, just-outside values, malformed input, whitespace and end-of-file. Record test IDs and expected outcomes before implementing the function.
hints: Derive tests from the contract, not only from the code you wrote.
For an inclusive range, test the lower bound, upper bound and values just outside them.
Include empty and single-element collections when relevant.
Calculate expected values independently so the test can detect a faulty implementation.
Keep a failing test after the bug is fixed; it becomes a regression test.
Use sanitizers and static analysis as complementary evidence, not as substitutes for a test plan.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest source for expected test results?
options: The requirement or contract, interpreted independently of the implementation
Whatever the program printed
A value chosen after the test failed
The first result from an unrelated program
questions.answer: The requirement or contract, interpreted independently of the implementation
questions.explanation: Expected results must come from the specified behaviour so the test can detect implementation mistakes.

questions.prompt: For an inclusive valid range 1 through 100, which values are especially useful boundary tests?
options: Only 50
Only 1 and 2
Only 99 and 100
questions.explanation: Testing just outside and exactly at both boundaries checks off-by-one conditions.

questions.prompt: Why keep a test that exposed a bug after fixing it?
options: It acts as a regression test to detect the same defect returning
It guarantees the entire program is correct
It replaces code review
It prevents future requirements from changing
questions.answer: It acts as a regression test to detect the same defect returning
questions.explanation: A retained failing-case test checks that the repaired behaviour remains correct.

questions.prompt: What does a passing test suite establish?
options: The tested observations passed; untested behaviour may still contain defects
The program is mathematically proven correct for all inputs
The compiler cannot generate a defect
The program is portable to every C implementation
questions.answer: The tested observations passed; untested behaviour may still contain defects
questions.explanation: Testing provides evidence for covered cases, not universal proof.

questions.prompt: Which tool is complementary to a test suite?
options: A sanitizer that can detect certain runtime memory and undefined-behaviour defects
A formatter that changes expected outputs
A setting that disables warnings
A random edit to the source
questions.answer: A sanitizer that can detect certain runtime memory and undefined-behaviour defects
questions.explanation: Sanitizers and static analysis add evidence but do not replace requirements-based tests.
